Pregnancy

Low-lying placenta: scans, bleeding and birth options

Updated: November 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A low placenta on a midpregnancy scan often changes position relative to the cervix as the uterus grows. Follow-up establishes whether it remains close to the birth canal. If you know your placenta is low and have bleeding, contractions or pain, contact your maternity service immediately. Heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain with bleeding, or feeling faint needs emergency help.

Understand the words on your scan report

The placenta attaches to the uterine wall and supports the exchange of oxygen, nutrients and waste between you and your baby. An anterior placenta is on the front wall; a posterior placenta is on the back. Either can also be low. These words describe different aspects of its location.

Low-lying generally means that the placental edge is less than 20 millimetres (2 centimetres) from the internal opening of the cervix. Placenta praevia means it reaches or covers that opening, partly or completely. The measurement is not 2 millimetres. Ask for the actual distance, whether there is overlap, and the pregnancy week when it was measured.

Why a later scan can give a different result

The lower uterus stretches as pregnancy progresses, changing the distance between the placenta and cervix. This does not mean the placenta detaches and slides around. NHS information reports that about nine in ten placentas found low at the midpregnancy scan are no longer low at follow-up.

That population figure is not a personal guarantee. A placenta covering the opening is less likely to clear it than one lying nearby; previous caesarean scarring and the stage of pregnancy also matter. There is no exercise, sleeping position or home treatment that moves it. Keep the planned scan even if you feel entirely well.

Why it happens, and what it does not tell you

Often there is no single explanation. Associations include previous caesarean or other uterine surgery, fertility treatment, smoking, older maternal age, multiple pregnancy and endometriosis. An association does not establish what caused an individual person’s placental position or predict their outcome.

Tell your team about previous operations and pregnancy complications. The finding is not a reliable way to identify your baby’s sex. Practical care depends on imaging and your health, not on a list of risk factors or blame for where implantation occurred.

Follow-up imaging and an internal ultrasound

Placental position is usually assessed at the midpregnancy anatomy scan, around 18–21 weeks. A common follow-up pathway is a scan at about 32 weeks, with another near 36 weeks if it remains low. Services may adjust this schedule according to the first measurement, symptoms and previous surgery.

A transvaginal scan places a probe inside the vagina to obtain a clearer view of the cervix and placental edge. It is considered safe when performed for this assessment, including when the placenta is low. The clinician should explain the examination and obtain your consent. Cervical length may also be measured to help assess the chance of early birth or bleeding.

Spotting and bleeding need an action plan

Placenta praevia can cause painless bleeding, sometimes after intercourse. The absence of pain does not make it safe to ignore. Bleeding can have another cause too, so do not diagnose it from its colour or amount. Contact your maternity team promptly for any spotting, contractions or pelvic pain when a low placenta is known.

Call your local emergency number for heavy bleeding, bleeding with severe abdominal pain, or bleeding with faintness, dizziness or collapse. Do not wait for the next scan. Clinicians may assess your circulation, examine you with consent, perform ultrasound and blood tests, and check your baby as appropriate to the pregnancy stage.

Sex, daily activity and care at home

Your clinician may advise avoiding vaginal penetration because it can trigger bleeding. If bleeding has occurred, avoid sex until you have been assessed and given advice. Ask exactly what any restriction covers and when it should be reviewed; a vague instruction to “take it easy” can leave important questions unanswered.

Ask separately about exercise, work, lifting and travel. Do not assume that staying in bed will change placental position. Some people without symptoms can be cared for at home, while bleeding or other concerns may make hospital observation appropriate. Keep the maternity contact number available and discuss transport, distance from hospital and help at home.

Medicines support care rather than moving the placenta

If early birth appears likely, corticosteroid injections may reduce complications of prematurity. They are most useful close to the expected birth, usually within the preceding week. They are not automatically needed just because a scan shows a low placenta, and they do not raise the placenta.

The decision depends on pregnancy stage, the likelihood of birth soon, previous treatment and your circumstances. Benefits and uncertainties differ later in pregnancy; diabetes may require extra glucose monitoring. In selected situations, clinicians may briefly use medicine to delay contractions so other treatment can be given. Urgent delivery must not be postponed simply to finish a medicine course.

Does a low placenta always mean a caesarean?

If the placenta still covers the cervical opening near birth, a caesarean is generally needed. If it has cleared the opening, the measured gap and the whole clinical picture matter. A scan from several months earlier cannot settle the final birth plan.

RCOG’s 2026 guideline recommends discussing a trial of labour for an asymptomatic low-lying placenta with an edge 11–20 millimetres from the opening after 36 weeks. This is an option for selected circumstances, not a guarantee. Older leaflets often give a blanket 20-millimetre caesarean rule; ask your obstetrician how current guidance, bleeding history and local facilities apply to you.

Agree when and where the birth should happen

Timing balances increasing bleeding risk against the effects of being born early. The 2026 RCOG guideline advises considering planned birth no later than 37 weeks and 6 days for an asymptomatic low-lying placenta or placenta praevia. Bleeding or other problems can require an earlier birth. Your team should give you a specific plan and explain what would change it.

Persistent praevia needs a hospital prepared to manage significant bleeding, with appropriate obstetric, anaesthetic and blood-transfusion support. If premature birth is likely, discuss newborn care too. A planned date does not replace the instruction to seek help for new symptoms beforehand.

Prepare for bleeding without assuming the worst

Ask about haemoglobin checks and treatment if iron deficiency is found. Follow the prescribed iron plan and report side effects rather than quietly abandoning it. Iron-rich food can support treatment, but does not move the placenta or stop an acute haemorrhage.

Your team should discuss possible transfusion and the measures available to control major bleeding. Occasionally, removal of the uterus is needed when bleeding cannot otherwise be controlled; this is not an inevitable outcome. Discuss blood-product preferences early. A low placenta over a previous caesarean scar may also prompt assessment for placenta accreta spectrum, a separate problem involving abnormal attachment.

Bring clear questions to the next appointment

Ask: What is the placental edge-to-cervix distance now? Is it covering the opening? When is the next scan? Do I need additional assessment because of a uterine scar? Which symptoms require an immediate call, and where should I go?

Then clarify the activity advice, proposed birth route and timing, and the backup plan for bleeding before that date. Keep these answers with your maternity records. The purpose of follow-up is to update decisions as the pregnancy changes, rather than to predict everything from the first scan.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

The 2026 RCOG guideline informs current birth options and timing; older public leaflets may differ.

Ultrasound follow-up distinguishes a temporary midpregnancy finding from a persistent low placenta.

Bleeding advice and treatment decisions require the maternity team’s assessment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you organize scan dates and questions. It cannot measure placental position, interpret bleeding or choose the timing or route of birth.

When to seek help

Seek immediate maternity advice for spotting, contractions or pain with a known low placenta. Call emergency services for heavy bleeding, bleeding with severe pain, or faintness or collapse. Do not wait for a scheduled scan.

Evidence notes updated: November 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A midpregnancy low placenta often clears the cervix, but follow-up confirms this.
  • The usual low-lying threshold is 20 millimetres, not 2 millimetres.
  • Report spotting, contractions or pain promptly; heavy bleeding or faintness needs emergency help.
  • Birth options depend on the latest scan, symptoms and individual assessment.

Frequently asked questions

Can I have intercourse with a low-lying placenta?

You may be advised to avoid vaginal penetration. If you have bleeding, avoid sex until assessed. Ask your team for specific advice and when to review it.

What should I do if I notice spotting?

Contact your maternity service immediately when a low placenta is known. Heavy bleeding, severe pain with bleeding, or faintness requires emergency help.

Will I definitely need a caesarean?

Not necessarily. A placenta covering the opening near birth generally requires one; a placenta nearby needs an individual discussion based on the latest scan.

Can vaginal birth be an option?

It may be, depending on the final placental position and your circumstances. Discuss the current guideline and your own bleeding history with the obstetric team.

Can resting or a special position make it move up?

There is no established home method to move the placenta. Follow your activity advice and attend repeat imaging.

Is an internal scan safe?

Transvaginal ultrasound is an accepted, safe way to measure placental position. The clinician should explain what it involves and ask for consent.

Do I automatically need steroid injections?

No. They are considered when premature birth is sufficiently likely and the expected benefits outweigh the risks for your pregnancy.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
